subtopics.title: Polymers, monomers and functionality
subtopics.theory_md:
A **polymer** is a macromolecule (molar mass about $10^4$ to $10^6$ g/mol) made by joining many small **monomers** with **covalent bonds**; the chains are held to each other by weaker van der Waals and hydrogen bonds. The repeat unit is the basic unit; the **degree of polymerisation** is $DP = M_{polymer}/M_{repeat\ unit}$.

**Functionality** is the number of bonding sites a monomer offers. A C=C counts as 2 (ethylene); each -OH, -COOH, -NH$_2$ counts as 1.
- Functionality 2 (ethylene, diol + diacid): **linear** polymer.
- Functionality 3 or more (glycerol, phenol towards HCHO): **branched or cross-linked** network.
- Functionality 1 (ethanol, acetic acid) or 0 (methane): no polymer; ethanol + acetic acid stop at ethyl acetate.

Natural polymers: cellulose, starch, proteins, natural rubber.
subtopics.basics_md: Think of a chain of paper clips. Each clip needs two free ends to join its neighbours. A monomer with only one free end can attach once and stop; one with three ends makes a net.

subtopics.title: Addition, condensation and copolymers
subtopics.theory_md:
**Addition (chain-growth)**: unsaturated monomers (C=C) add with **no by-product**; polymer has the same empirical formula as the monomer, $M = n M_0$. Needs an initiator, fast. Examples: polyethylene, PVC, polystyrene, Teflon.

**Condensation (step-growth)**: monomers with two different functional groups react with **loss of a small molecule** ($\mathrm{H_2O}$, HCl). Slow, stepwise; repeat unit differs from monomers. Examples: nylon 6,6 (hexamethylenediamine + adipic acid, $-\mathrm{H_2O}$), terylene (glycol + terephthalic acid), bakelite.

**Copolymerisation**: two or more different monomers in one chain (Buna-S: butadiene + styrene); random, alternating, block or graft.

Cellulose nitrate is made by nitrating cellulose, not by addition polymerisation.

subtopics.title: Thermodynamic feasibility and ceiling temperature
subtopics.theory_md:
Polymerisation is feasible only if $\Delta G_p = \Delta H_p - T\Delta S_p < 0$.

- $\Delta S_p$ is **negative**: free monomers become one chain, so freedom is lost.
- $\Delta H_p$ is **negative** (exothermic): one $\pi$ bond becomes a stronger $\sigma$ bond, releasing about 35 to 100 kJ/mol.
- So polymerisation is favoured at **low temperature**. Above the **ceiling temperature** $T_c = \Delta H_p/\Delta S_p$, $\Delta G_p>0$ and the polymer depolymerises.

Ethylene: $\Delta H_p=-93$ kJ/mol, $\Delta S_p=-155$ J/(mol K). At 298 K, $\Delta G_p = -93000 + 298\times155 = -46\,810$ J/mol, so it polymerises; $T_c = 93000/155 = 600$ K.
subtopics.basics_md: A reaction goes ahead if it lowers free energy. Joining molecules into a chain cuts disorder (bad) but forms stronger bonds (good); the bond gain must win.

subtopics.title: Tacticity: isotactic, syndiotactic, atactic
subtopics.theory_md:
**Tacticity** is the spatial arrangement of the side groups R along a chain $\mathrm{-[CH_2-CHR]_n-}$. It exists because each CHR carbon is **asymmetric (chiral)**. It is a **configuration** (set when the polymer forms, changed only by breaking bonds), unlike linear, branched or cross-linked, which describe chain architecture.

| Type | Side groups | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Isotactic | all on the same side | crystalline, strong, high m.p. |
| Syndiotactic | alternate regularly | crystalline |
| Atactic | random | amorphous, soft, tacky |

Isotactic PP (m.p. about 165 $^\circ$C) is made with Ziegler-Natta catalyst; atactic PP is a weak, sticky material.

subtopics.title: Free radical addition polymerisation
subtopics.theory_md:
A chain reaction in three steps. **Initiators**: benzoyl peroxide, AIBN, $\mathrm{H_2O_2}$, persulphate (heat or light makes radicals $\mathrm{R^\bullet}$).

1. **Initiation**: $\mathrm{(C_6H_5COO)_2 \xrightarrow{\Delta} 2C_6H_5COO^\bullet \rightarrow 2C_6H_5^\bullet + 2CO_2}$, then $\mathrm{R^\bullet + CH_2{=}CH_2 \rightarrow R{-}CH_2{-}CH_2^\bullet}$.
2. **Propagation**: the radical adds monomer after monomer, $\mathrm{R{-}CH_2CH_2^\bullet + n\,CH_2{=}CH_2 \rightarrow R{-}(CH_2CH_2)_n{-}CH_2CH_2^\bullet}$.
3. **Termination**: two radicals meet, by **coupling** (join) or **disproportionation** (H transfer, one chain gets a C=C and one is saturated).

Gives LDPE, PVC, polystyrene, PMMA. High molar mass forms from the start; monomer is used up slowly.
subtopics.basics_md: A radical is an atom with an unpaired electron that wants a partner. It grabs the C=C electrons of a monomer, which leaves a new radical at the end of the chain, and so on.

subtopics.title: Cationic and anionic polymerisation
subtopics.theory_md:
Both need **dry, oxygen-free** conditions and low temperature.

**Cationic**: initiator a Lewis acid + co-catalyst ($\mathrm{BF_3 + H_2O}$, $\mathrm{AlCl_3}$); monomers with **electron-donating** groups (isobutylene, vinyl ethers); the growing end is a carbocation; ends by loss of $\mathrm{H^+}$.

**Anionic**: initiator a strong base/nucleophile (n-BuLi, $\mathrm{NaNH_2}$, sodium naphthalene); monomers with **electron-withdrawing** groups (styrene, acrylonitrile, MMA); the growing end is a carbanion, solvent THF.

Steps: initiation, propagation, termination. **No termination in anionic** (carbanions repel) gives **living polymers**: growth continues on adding monomer and is stopped by water or alcohol.

Anionic, DP 2: $\mathrm{Bu^-} + \mathrm{CH_2{=}CHPh} \rightarrow \mathrm{Bu{-}CH_2CH(Ph)^-}$; one more styrene gives $\mathrm{Bu(CH_2CHPh)_2^-}$; $\mathrm{H_2O}$ gives the dimer.

subtopics.title: Ziegler-Natta coordination polymerisation
subtopics.theory_md:
**Catalyst**: $\mathrm{TiCl_4 + Al(C_2H_5)_3}$ (Ziegler-Natta), used for ethylene and propylene at low pressure.

1. **Active site**: $\mathrm{TiCl_4 + Al(C_2H_5)_3 \rightarrow Cl_3Ti{-}C_2H_5 + Al(C_2H_5)_2Cl}$ (alkyl moves to Ti, leaving a vacant site).
2. **Coordination**: monomer binds to the vacant site.
3. **Insertion**: monomer inserts into the Ti-alkyl bond, so the alkyl group becomes the chain end: $\mathrm{[Ti]{-}R + CH_2{=}CHCH_3 \rightarrow [Ti]{-}CH_2CH(CH_3){-}R}$.
4. Repeated; stops with $\mathrm{H_2}$.

Hence also called **insertion polymerisation**. The surface fixes monomer orientation: linear, **isotactic** product (HDPE, isotactic PP), more crystalline and stronger but less transparent. Unlike ionic, there are no free ions and it controls stereochemistry.
subtopics.basics_md: The monomer docks at a metal atom, which holds it in one orientation, and then slides into the metal-carbon bond. Every unit enters the same way, so the chain is regular.

subtopics.title: Number average and weight average molar mass
subtopics.theory_md:
A polymer sample has chains of many lengths (**polydisperse**), so molar mass is an average. For $N_i$ molecules of molar mass $M_i$:

$$\overline{M}_n=\frac{\sum N_iM_i}{\sum N_i}\qquad \overline{M}_w=\frac{\sum N_iM_i^2}{\sum N_iM_i}=\sum w_iM_i$$

$w_i$ is the weight fraction of species $i$. $\overline{M}_n$ counts every molecule equally (found by osmometry or end-group analysis); $\overline{M}_w$ gives heavy chains more weight (light scattering). Units g/mol.

Example: 100 molecules of 10 000 and 100 of 30 000 g/mol: $\overline{M}_n=20\,000$, $\overline{M}_w=25\,000$ g/mol.

subtopics.title: Polydispersity index and degree of polymerisation
subtopics.theory_md:
**Polydispersity index** $PDI=\overline{M}_w/\overline{M}_n\ge 1$. Because
$$\overline{M}_w-\overline{M}_n=\frac{\sigma^2}{\overline{M}_n}\ge 0,$$
where $\sigma^2$ is the variance of the distribution, $\overline{M}_w\ge\overline{M}_n$; equality ($PDI=1$) holds only for a **monodisperse** sample (all chains equal, as in proteins). Living anionic polymers give $PDI$ near 1; free radical and condensation polymers about 2.

A larger PDI means a broader distribution. Higher molar mass gives more strength, toughness and melt viscosity; low-mass chains act like plasticiser and lower strength.

$DP=\overline{M}_n/M_0$ ($M_0$ = repeat-unit mass).

subtopics.title: Thermoplastic versus thermosetting
subtopics.theory_md:
**Thermoplastics** (PE, PVC, polystyrene, nylon): linear or branched chains held by weak van der Waals or H-bond forces. They soften on heating, harden on cooling, **reversibly**, so can be remoulded and recycled; soluble in solvents; softer, tougher.

**Thermosets** (bakelite, urea-formaldehyde, epoxy): on first heating (curing) chains join by **covalent cross-links** into a 3-D network. They do not soften again, char on strong heating, are insoluble, hard, rigid and brittle.

**Cross-linking** = covalent bonds between chains. PVC with plasticizer is soft; bakelite is hard and brittle because chains cannot slide.
subtopics.basics_md: Thermoplastic is like candle wax: melt and reshape again. Thermoset is like a baked cake: once set, heat only burns it.
key_points: Thermoplastic: linear, weak forces, softens reversibly, recyclable
Thermoset: 3-D covalent network, permanent set, insoluble, hard and brittle

subtopics.title: Role of gypsum
subtopics.theory_md:
$\mathrm{C_3A}$ reacts with water at once and releases a lot of heat, so cement would **flash set** and could not be placed. **Gypsum** ($\mathrm{CaSO_4\cdot2H_2O}$, 2 to 3%, added during grinding of clinker) reacts with C$_3$A to form insoluble **ettringite** (calcium sulphoaluminate) which coats the C$_3$A grains and **retards** hydration:

$\mathrm{3CaO\cdot Al_2O_3 + 3(CaSO_4\cdot2H_2O)+26H_2O \rightarrow 3CaO\cdot Al_2O_3\cdot3CaSO_4\cdot32H_2O}$

This gives an initial setting time of at least 30 min. Excess gypsum causes expansion and unsoundness.

questions.q: Carbonation of concrete
Why does low water-cement ratio improve durability of RCC?
questions.model_answer_md: Less water leaves fewer pores, so concrete is dense and impermeable. Water, chlorides and $\mathrm{CO_2}$ cannot reach the steel, carbonation is slow, the steel stays passive and does not rust and crack the cover.

questions.q: Which cement is recommended for a bridge in constant moisture?

points: Cement: PPC/slag or sulphate resisting; pozzolana gives extra C-S-H
Concrete: M30-M40, low w/c about 0.4, curing; cover 45-50 mm, coated bars
Mechanism: low permeability, steel stays passive, slows carbonation and chloride attack, avoids rust expansion cracking
